title: Business English Essentials
description: Core vocabulary every professional needs — strategy, leadership, communication, and execution.

words.definitionEn: To use something to maximum advantage in a given situation.
words.exampleSentence: We can leverage our existing customer relationships to expand into new markets.
words.nuance: More strategic and intentional than simply 'use' — implies smart deployment of an existing advantage.
words.realLifeTask: In your next status update, replace 'use' with 'leverage' when describing how your team is applying a resource.

words.definitionEn: A standard or point of reference against which performance or quality is measured.
words.exampleSentence: We need to benchmark our onboarding process against industry leaders.
words.nuance: Used both as a noun (set a benchmark) and a verb (to benchmark something). Common in performance reviews and product strategy.
words.realLifeTask: Mention a benchmark in your next report: 'Our NPS is 42, which benchmarks well against the industry average of 35.'

words.definitionEn: A person or group with an interest in, or affected by, a business decision or project.
words.exampleSentence: We need to align all key stakeholders before moving to the next phase.
words.nuance: Broader than 'shareholder' — includes clients, employees, managers, and external partners. Essential in project and product language.
words.realLifeTask: In your next project doc, list three stakeholders and their interests in one sentence each.

words.definitionEn: To make a process easier or more likely to happen; to help something run smoothly.
words.exampleSentence: The new platform will facilitate collaboration across remote teams.
words.nuance: More formal and professional than 'help'. Often used for systems, processes, or meetings: 'facilitate a workshop', 'facilitate change'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'facilitate' in a sentence about your next meeting or project: 'This tool will facilitate faster decision-making.'

words.definitionEn: To put a decision, plan, or system into effect; to execute something that has been planned.
words.exampleSentence: The team will implement the new feedback process starting next quarter.
words.nuance: Implies that planning is complete and action is now being taken. More formal than 'do' or 'start'.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one thing you are currently implementing at work in a sentence.

words.definitionEn: A concrete output, result, or product that must be produced as part of a project.
words.exampleSentence: The main deliverables for Q3 are the redesigned onboarding flow and the updated pricing page.
words.nuance: Specific to project management language — a deliverable is tangible and has a deadline, unlike a vague 'goal'.
words.realLifeTask: List two deliverables for your current project in one sentence each.

words.definitionEn: Able to be expanded or adapted to handle greater volume, complexity, or growth without loss of quality.
words.exampleSentence: We need a scalable solution that can handle ten times our current user base.
words.nuance: A key word in tech, product, and startup environments. Often contrasted with solutions that work now but break under growth.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one aspect of your current work or product as 'scalable' or 'not yet scalable' in a sentence.

words.definitionEn: To arrange tasks or goals in order of importance so that the most critical ones are addressed first.
words.exampleSentence: We need to prioritise customer retention over acquiring new users this quarter.
words.nuance: Common in any planning or decision-making context. Note: 'prioritize' is American English; 'prioritise' is British English.
words.realLifeTask: In your next planning meeting, say: 'Let's prioritise [X] because [reason].'

words.definitionEn: To bring different people, teams, or goals into agreement or coordination with each other.
words.exampleSentence: Before we proceed, we need to align with the marketing team on the messaging.
words.nuance: Very common in business. 'Are we aligned?' is a quick way to ask if everyone agrees. Overused in some environments — use with awareness.
words.realLifeTask: Ask a colleague: 'Are we aligned on the timeline for this?' and notice their reaction.

words.definitionEn: To make a significant change in strategy, direction, or approach while keeping the core goal.
words.exampleSentence: After losing the key contract, we had to pivot our entire sales strategy.
words.nuance: Popularised by startup culture. Can sound overused in some contexts, but remains standard vocabulary for describing strategic changes.
words.realLifeTask: Describe a time your team had to pivot on a project in two or three sentences.

words.definitionEn: A point in a process that is slower than the rest and causes delays or congestion.
words.exampleSentence: The bottleneck in our pipeline is the manual approval step — it delays releases by three days.
words.nuance: From manufacturing (a narrow bottle neck slows liquid flow). Now universal in project management, product development, and operations.
words.realLifeTask: Identify one bottleneck in your current workflow and describe it in a sentence.

words.definitionEn: Taking action to prevent problems before they occur, rather than reacting after the fact.
words.exampleSentence: A proactive approach to customer service means anticipating issues before users report them.
words.nuance: Contrasted with 'reactive'. Very common in performance reviews and leadership discussions. Becoming slightly overused but still essential vocabulary.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one proactive step you took this week at work.

words.definitionEn: To make a process more efficient and effective by simplifying or removing unnecessary steps.
words.exampleSentence: The new tool will streamline our reporting process and save the team five hours per week.
words.nuance: Implies both simplification and speed improvement. Often used in operations, HR, and product contexts.
words.realLifeTask: Identify one process you could streamline at work and explain how in two sentences.

words.definitionEn: A significant stage or point of achievement in the progress of a project or goal.
words.exampleSentence: Reaching 10,000 active users was a major milestone for our product team.
words.nuance: Different from a deadline (which is time-based) or a task (which is small). A milestone marks a significant achievement or decision point.
words.realLifeTask: Name three milestones in your current project in a short list.

words.definitionEn: To refer an issue to a higher authority for resolution; or to increase in intensity.
words.exampleSentence: If the client doesn't respond within 48 hours, please escalate this to the account director.
words.nuance: Has two common uses: (1) moving an issue upward in an organisation, (2) a situation getting more serious. The first is the professional standard use.
words.realLifeTask: Practise saying: 'I'll need to escalate this if we don't have a resolution by Friday.'

words.definitionEn: The key point, lesson, or conclusion that you want an audience to remember from a meeting or presentation.
words.exampleSentence: The main takeaway from today's retrospective is that we need clearer ownership of tasks.
words.nuance: Common in business communication. Often used at the end of a presentation or meeting: 'The key takeaways are...'
words.realLifeTask: After your next meeting, write down the three main takeaways in bullet points.

words.definitionEn: Clear, definite, and able to be measured or demonstrated — not vague or abstract.
words.exampleSentence: We need tangible results by the end of the quarter, not just progress reports.
words.nuance: Often contrasted with 'intangible' benefits. Used to demand or demonstrate results that can actually be seen or measured.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one tangible outcome from your last project in one sentence.

words.definitionEn: Openness and honesty about decisions, processes, and information within an organisation.
words.exampleSentence: The team appreciated the leadership's transparency about the restructuring plans.
words.nuance: A value frequently cited in company cultures. Can also refer to being transparent with data (visibility) or process (no hidden steps).
words.realLifeTask: Use 'transparency' in a sentence about communication in your workplace.

words.definitionEn: The obligation to take responsibility for one's actions and the outcomes they produce.
words.exampleSentence: Creating a culture of accountability means that everyone knows what they own and follows through.
words.nuance: Different from 'responsibility' — accountability implies being answerable to others, not just to yourself. Often paired with 'ownership'.
words.realLifeTask: In your next 1:1, clarify who has accountability for one open action item.

words.definitionEn: A new plan or programme designed to solve a problem or achieve a goal; also the ability to act independently.
words.exampleSentence: The company launched a new initiative to improve internal knowledge sharing.
words.nuance: Can mean a specific project ('a new initiative') or a personal quality ('she shows great initiative'). Context makes the meaning clear.
words.realLifeTask: Describe a current initiative at your company in two sentences.

words.definitionEn: General agreement among a group of people, especially after discussion.
words.exampleSentence: After an hour of debate, the team reached a consensus on the product roadmap.
words.nuance: Not unanimous agreement — consensus means most people agree enough to move forward. Common in decision-making contexts.
words.realLifeTask: In your next meeting, ask: 'Do we have consensus on this, or are there concerns we should address first?'

words.definitionEn: Strong, effective, and able to perform well even under pressure or in difficult conditions.
words.exampleSentence: We need a more robust process for handling customer complaints at scale.
words.nuance: Frequently used in business to describe systems, plans, or frameworks that are well-built and won't break under stress.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one robust and one fragile process at your workplace in a sentence each.

words.definitionEn: Capable of working successfully; practical and realistic given available resources.
words.exampleSentence: Building a custom solution in-house isn't viable given our current budget and timeline.
words.nuance: Often used in phrases like 'viable option', 'commercially viable', 'minimum viable product (MVP)'.
words.realLifeTask: Assess one option for a current project: 'This approach is/isn't viable because…'

words.definitionEn: Progress or momentum, especially the early signs that a product, idea, or project is succeeding.
words.exampleSentence: The new feature has been gaining traction with our enterprise clients.
words.nuance: Common in startup and product language. 'Gaining traction' means things are starting to work and grow.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one area of your work that is gaining traction this month.

words.definitionEn: Detailed and specific, involving examination at the level of small individual elements.
words.exampleSentence: Can we get more granular data on which user segments are churning?
words.nuance: Common in data, analytics, and strategy conversations. 'Getting granular' means diving into the details. Use when asking for more depth.
words.realLifeTask: Ask for granular information in your next data review: 'Can we break this down at a more granular level?'

words.definitionEn: Considering the whole system or situation rather than focusing on individual parts in isolation.
words.exampleSentence: We need a holistic view of the customer journey, not just the conversion funnel.
words.nuance: Often used to advocate for a broader view in discussions where people are too focused on one metric or process.
words.realLifeTask: Describe a problem at work from a holistic perspective, connecting at least two different departments or factors.

words.definitionEn: Practical and specific enough to be acted upon immediately; ready to be turned into concrete steps.
words.exampleSentence: The report needs to end with actionable recommendations, not just observations.
words.nuance: Key word in business communication — distinguishes useful information from information that doesn't lead anywhere. 'Make it actionable' is a common request.
words.realLifeTask: Turn one vague goal into an actionable next step: 'Instead of improve NPS, we will call 5 detractors this week.'

words.definitionEn: To repeat and refine a process or design through multiple cycles, improving with each round.
words.exampleSentence: We'll launch a basic version first and iterate based on user feedback.
words.nuance: Central to agile and product development thinking. Implies that perfection isn't the first goal — learning and improving is.
words.realLifeTask: Describe a process at work that you iterate on regularly.

words.definitionEn: To integrate a new employee, client, or user into a system or organisation.
words.exampleSentence: It takes about six weeks to fully onboard a new enterprise client.
words.nuance: Used for both employees (HR onboarding) and customers (product onboarding). As a noun: 'onboarding process', 'onboarding flow'.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one improvement you would make to your current onboarding process in two sentences.

words.definitionEn: The available capacity a person or team has to take on additional work or responsibilities.
words.exampleSentence: I don't have the bandwidth to take on a new project before the end of the month.
words.nuance: A metaphor from network technology — now standard in workplace language. Saying you lack bandwidth politely signals you are at capacity without saying 'I'm too busy'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'bandwidth' this week when discussing your workload: 'Do we have the bandwidth to take this on?'

words.definitionEn: A structured system, set of principles, or approach used to guide decisions or organise work.
words.exampleSentence: We use the RICE framework to score and prioritise features on our roadmap.
words.nuance: Can refer to a methodology (Agile framework), a mental model, or a document structure. Very flexible term in professional language.
words.realLifeTask: Mention a framework you use at work in a sentence: 'We use [X] framework to help us make decisions about [Y].'

words.definitionEn: The process of gradually introducing or deploying a new product, feature, or change.
words.exampleSentence: The feature rollout will start with 10% of users and scale to 100% over two weeks.
words.nuance: Implies phased or staged introduction rather than an instant switch. Common in product, IT, and marketing contexts.
words.realLifeTask: Describe the rollout plan for something you are currently working on.

words.definitionEn: A persistent or recurring problem that causes difficulty for customers, clients, or team members.
words.exampleSentence: The biggest pain point for enterprise clients is the complexity of the current integration process.
words.nuance: Widely used in sales, customer research, and product development. Identifying pain points is the first step to solving problems.
words.realLifeTask: Name three pain points your users or clients experience with your current product or service.

words.definitionEn: A clear statement of the specific benefit a product or service delivers to its users or customers.
words.exampleSentence: Our value proposition is simple: save users three hours a week on manual reporting.
words.nuance: More specific and outcome-focused than a general description. A strong value proposition answers: 'Why should I choose you over alternatives?'
words.realLifeTask: Write your product or team's value proposition in one sentence.

words.definitionEn: A strategic plan showing the goals, milestones, and timeline for achieving a product or business objective.
words.exampleSentence: The product roadmap for H2 focuses on enterprise integrations and mobile performance.
words.nuance: Widely used in product management and engineering. A roadmap is directional, not a fixed contract — it changes based on new information.
words.realLifeTask: Describe one item on your current roadmap and why it was prioritised.

words.definitionEn: A method of solving a problem by bypassing the root cause rather than fixing it directly.
words.exampleSentence: Until the bug is fixed, we've implemented a workaround that manually resets the sync every hour.
words.nuance: Implies a pragmatic but imperfect solution. Useful for acknowledging constraints while still moving forward. Not a long-term strategy.
words.realLifeTask: Describe a workaround currently in use in your work and what the permanent fix would look like.

words.definitionEn: Formal approval given by someone with authority before a project, document, or decision moves forward.
words.exampleSentence: We're waiting for sign-off from legal before we can launch the campaign.
words.nuance: Signals the end of a review cycle and the beginning of execution. 'Who needs to sign off on this?' is a key governance question.
words.realLifeTask: Identify who needs to sign off on your next deliverable and what they typically need to see before approving.

words.definitionEn: An advance warning or early notice about something that is going to happen.
words.exampleSentence: Just a heads-up: the client is visiting on Thursday, so the office should be ready.
words.nuance: Informal but very common in workplace communication. Usually given out of courtesy or to allow the recipient time to prepare.
words.realLifeTask: Give someone at work a heads-up today: 'Just wanted to give you a heads-up that [X] is happening.'

words.definitionEn: To draw attention to something important that needs to be noticed, discussed, or addressed.
words.exampleSentence: I wanted to flag a potential risk before it becomes a problem for the team.
words.nuance: Common in business communication for raising concerns in a polite, non-confrontational way. 'I just wanted to flag this' is softer than 'This is a problem'.
words.realLifeTask: Practise flagging an issue in your next team meeting: 'I wanted to flag a concern about [X].'

words.definitionEn: The time required to complete a task and return a result; or a complete reversal of a negative situation.
words.exampleSentence: We guarantee a 48-hour turnaround on all client feedback requests.
words.nuance: Has two distinct meanings: (1) time to complete (turnaround time), (2) a company or situation recovering from failure (business turnaround).
words.realLifeTask: What is the typical turnaround time for one key task in your role? State it in a sentence.

words.definitionEn: To carefully adjust or fine-tune an approach, expectation, or process to ensure accuracy.
words.exampleSentence: We need to calibrate our targets for Q4 based on the slower-than-expected H1 growth.
words.nuance: Originally a scientific term (calibrating instruments). Now widely used in business for adjusting expectations, goals, and messages.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'calibrate' in a sentence about adjusting a goal or expectation at work.

words.definitionEn: To distribute or send a document, message, or information to a group of people.
words.exampleSentence: Could you circulate the meeting agenda at least 24 hours in advance?
words.nuance: More formal than 'share' or 'send'. Implies structured distribution to a defined group. Often used for formal documents.
words.realLifeTask: Circulate a document or agenda for your next meeting and mention that you have done so.

words.definitionEn: To examine something in progressively greater detail; to move from a high-level view into specifics.
words.exampleSentence: The overall numbers look healthy, but let's drill down into the regional data.
words.nuance: Common in data, analytics, and business intelligence contexts. Suggests going beyond surface-level information to understand the cause.
words.realLifeTask: In your next data review, say: 'Let's drill down into [specific metric] to understand what's driving this.'

words.definitionEn: The combined effect of two or more things working together that is greater than the sum of individual parts.
words.exampleSentence: The merger will create significant synergies between the two product lines.
words.nuance: One of the most overused words in business. Use it accurately — it specifically means 2+2=5, not just 'working together'. If possible, quantify the synergy.
words.realLifeTask: Identify one genuine synergy between two teams or products at your company.

words.definitionEn: The support, agreement, and commitment from key decision-makers needed before a project can move forward.
words.exampleSentence: Getting stakeholder buy-in early means fewer surprises and slower decisions later.
words.nuance: More than just approval — buy-in implies active support and willingness to contribute resources or political capital.
words.realLifeTask: Think of a current project. Who are the three stakeholders whose buy-in you need most?

words.definitionEn: Tasks, opportunities, or goals that are easily achievable and deliver quick results without much effort.
words.exampleSentence: Before we tackle the big infrastructure overhaul, let's pick off the low-hanging fruit and fix the three most common user errors.
words.nuance: Not necessarily unimportant — it simply signals something achievable now. Often the best place to start when building momentum.
words.realLifeTask: Identify three pieces of low-hanging fruit in your current project or role.

words.definitionEn: An advantage that makes a company, product, or person more successful than its competition.
words.exampleSentence: Our competitive edge is the depth of integrations we offer — no other tool in this space has more than twenty.
words.nuance: Similar to 'unique selling point' but broader — it covers any sustainable advantage, not just a single feature.
words.realLifeTask: Describe your team's or company's competitive edge in one or two sentences.

words.definitionEn: A deep and accurate understanding of a situation, problem, or audience, often revealed through data or experience.
words.exampleSentence: The customer interviews gave us a key insight: users don't abandon the product — they just forget to return.
words.nuance: More powerful than just 'information'. An insight is something that changes how you think or act. 'Insights from data' is different from 'data'.
words.realLifeTask: Share one insight from your most recent project or client interaction with a colleague.

words.definitionEn: A person, event, or thing that triggers or accelerates a change or process.
words.exampleSentence: The negative press coverage was actually a catalyst for the company to improve its support process.
words.nuance: From chemistry (a substance that speeds up a reaction). In business, it's something that causes change to happen faster than it would otherwise.
words.realLifeTask: Describe a catalyst for change in your organisation or industry in two sentences.

words.definitionEn: To publicly recommend or support a cause, policy, or person; also a person who does this.
words.exampleSentence: As a product manager, you need to advocate for the user in every business decision.
words.nuance: In business, being an 'advocate' for something implies active, visible support — going beyond passive agreement.
words.realLifeTask: Identify something or someone you need to advocate for in your current role.

words.definitionEn: The maximum amount of work, output, or activity that a person, team, or system can handle.
words.exampleSentence: We're already at full capacity — adding another project will require either more resource or a scope reduction.
words.nuance: Different from 'bandwidth' (which is more informal and personal). Capacity is more often used for systems, teams, or infrastructure.
words.realLifeTask: Assess your team's current capacity honestly: are you at 60%, 80%, or 100%?

words.definitionEn: Resistance or obstacles in a process that slow things down or cause difficulty for users or teams.
words.exampleSentence: We reduced sign-up friction by removing the email confirmation step and saw a 30% uplift in conversions.
words.nuance: From physics (resistance between surfaces). In business, friction is anything that makes a process harder or slower than it should be. Especially common in product and UX.
words.realLifeTask: Identify one source of friction in a process your users or customers experience and suggest how to reduce it.
